questions.title_en: Chanukah candles or Shabbos candles first on Friday
questions.question:
On Friday of Chanukah, the Kaf Hachaim O.C 679:1 says that it's because of מעלין בקודש (going up in holiness), so therefore Chanukah goes first and then Shabbat.

Why and in what way is Chanukah lighting less important in Kedushah than Shabbat candles?

answers.text:
In שער הכוונות דרוש חנוכה דרוש א Rav Chaim Vital writes:

״ואמנם נבאר תחילה ענין קדושת הימים האלו ואח"כ נבאר ענין ברכות נר של חנוכה. והנה כמו שנתבאר שבשבתות ויו"ט ור"ח יש בהם תוספת קדושה על ימי החול -- גם בחנוכה ופורים יש בהם תוספת קדושה יותר מימי החול. אמנם אין מדריגתם שוה למדריגת השבתות ויו"ט ור"ח."

“We will first explain the concept of the sanctity of these days, and afterward we will explain the matter of the blessings over the Chanukah lamp. Just as it has been explained that Shabbat, Festivals, and Rosh Chodesh possess an added sanctity beyond that of weekdays, so too Chanukah and Purim possess an added sanctity greater than that of weekdays. However, their level of sanctity is not equal to the level of Shabbat, Festivals, and Rosh Chodesh.”

In שער הכוונות דרוש חנוכה דרוש א he goes on to explain that Chanukah and Purim are rooted in the Sefira of הוד (splendour). I then saw in Pardes Rimonim 23:21 and other kabbalistic Seforim that it says that Shabbat is rooted in the sefira of מלכות, which is called the שכינה. Therefore, perhaps it would seem that solely based on where Shabbat is rooted within the sefirot (מלכות) and what it corresponds to, Shabbat would have more kedusha as it is representative of the שכינה.

questions.title_en: Were the 1st born Egyptians given a way out to avoid being killed in final plague of 1st born?
questions.question: Were the 1st born Egyptians given a way out to avoid being killed in plague of 1st born? Could they have converted or even smeared lamb's blood on their doorpost?

answers.text:
According to Midrash Hagadol the firstborn were not given a way to save their lives. It happened because either in Egypt they worshiped the first born and the decree to destroy the idols fell upon the firstborn; or because the pharaoh's heart was hardened and he would not change his decree. As quoted in the Katz Passover Haggada, according to Midrash haGadol Bo 11:5:

The firstborn hearing of the coming plague wanted their fathers to release the Jews. When the fathers refused, the firstborn fought against them and killed 600,000 of their fathers.

Unfortunately, it did not help and the (same midrash) says:

All firstborn died men and women. The firstborn either of father or of mother died.

The exceptions were according Midrash haGadol Bo 12:29 and Shemos Rabba 18:3:

Only two first born were left alive: Pharaoh and his daughter Batya, who saved Moshe from Nile river.

The extent of punishment was such that Midrash haGadol Bo 12:30

Dogs dug up firstborn that had died in the past and mutilated their bodies.

Also Yalkut Shimoni Bo 186 says that

The pictures of the dead firstborn turned to dust.

questions.title_en: R' Chaninah ben Dosa's table in Olam haBa
questions.question: Where can one find the story about R' Chaninah ben Dosa, that his table in Olam haBa had three gold legs instead of four, or two gold legs instead of three legs? How can we understand this story, if Olam haBa is not physical?

answers.text:
The source of the story is Taanit 25a, where Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa is extremely poor. His wife asks him to pray for something, he prays and receives a golden table leg. His wife sees in a dream that in the future he would be eating on a table of two legs instead of three, so she asks him to pray to have it taken back.

One interpretation is that the three legs of the table correspond to the three pillars the world stands on - Torah, prayer and acts of kindness (Avot 1:2). By living a comfortable life, Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa would be giving up on the constant need to pray, and would therefore be lacking the merit of prayer in the world to come (Maharsha). Or, if he chose to use his merit to have enough for himself, instead of using his merit to support the entire rest of the world, he would be lacking the pillar of acts of kindness, since he would no longer be providing for the rest of the world's livelihood (Ruach Chayyim, Avot 1:3).

Kashrut will not be completely gone. We will still have to check lettuce for bugs. At first, some die-hards will invoke mar'it ayin to reject eating fake meat in public, but this can't last long as new practices become widely known. Of course, if the Temple is rebuilt, we are enjoined to resume the sacrifices (and eat them in some cases), and in particular eat the Paschal lamb. But midrashic sources say that in the time to come all sacrifices will be abolished, except for the Thanksgiving sacrifice [Lev. R. 9:7], and the Talmud quotes God as saying that if we study the Torah portions dealing with sacrifices, He will count it as if we has actually done the sacrifices [Menachot 110].

Am I missing something in this analysis?

questions.title_en: Is there a connection between the sefirot and the flower of life symbol
questions.question:
Do the Sephirot and the Flower of Life refer to the same concept?

The Flower of Life symbol is found in archeology in Masada and the Galilee.

The Germ of Life is a small cross-section of the larger Flower of Life symbol. It’s often found on ancient Jewish tombs.

The Flower of Life is found all over the world, but considering it’s found in Israel, there must be some connection to Jewish mysticism.

Also, the word “sephirot” is similar to “sphere”, which is the 3d representation of the circles of the flower of life.

answers.text:
There’s no known connection. If there ever was one, nobody knows it today.

The Flower of Life is a symbol found in archeological sites throughout the Old World. It’s been interpreted variously. Its intended meaning was likely different depending on where it popped up, and in many cases it might just be an artistic motif. It’s presence in some ancient Israelite synagogues was likely an example of the latter, as there is no known Kabbalistic reference to the Flower of Life.

The Sephirot—also called מַאֲמרוֹת, דִּבּוּרִים, שֵׁמוֹת, אוֹרוֹת, כֹחוֹת, and כְּתָרִים—are a representation of the ten Divine Traits in Kabbalistic thought, only definitively attested from the First Century.

The connection of the word “Sephirah” to “Sphere” is untenable. Firstly, the only reasonable connection is for the term to have been borrowed from Koine Greek sphéra; and that would likely have resulted in Rabbinic Hebrew ’esfḗrā, rather than our safīrā́. Secondly, Sephirot have nothing to do with spheres, except if you count some written representations as two-dimensional circles.

Lastly, the presence of an artifact in Israel does not in any way indicate a special connection to Jewish mysticism. That’s not a logical conclusion. Nothing about being crafted by Jews inherently suggests a connection to Kabbalah.

questions.title_en: How many Mishna-Gemara segments appear in the Babylonian Talmud?
questions.question:
In the Babylonian Talmud, each chapter contains a Mishna and Gemara unit. The breakdown and usage of the Mishnayot, as compared to the original corpus, is frequently different. The roughly 4,192 Mishnayot in the original corpus of the six orders of the Mishna are not all used in the Babylonian Talmud. However, how many Mishnah-Gemara sections are there in in the Babylonian Talmud. The figure must be far less the 4000, for two of the six orders of the Mishna were basically excluded from the corpus of the Babylonian Talmud. But it may be considerably less than the strict figure of: 2,582

Moed: 418 Nashim: 521 Nezikin: 613 Kodashim: 1,030

simply due to the fact that the Mishnayot were restructured, as mentioned above.

I am similarly inquiring into the median word count, as well as a readout of the longest to shortest Mishna-Gemara segments.

questions.title_en: Why did God not want Jacob to know that Joseph was alive?
questions.question:
The Midrash says:

[The brothers] decided: “Let us make a vow to excommunicate any one of us who tells our father, Jacob, that Joseph is alive.” Judah said: “Reuben is not here, and a vow of excommunication cannot be executed unless ten witnesses are present.” So what did they do? They included the Holy One, blessed be He, in their pact of excommunication [and God agreed]. [Midrash Tanchuma, Vayeshev 2:5]

So God agreed that Jacob must not be told. Another Midrash tells us that Jacob’s father Isaac knew prophetically that Joseph was alive, but said nothing:

The Torah says: And all of Jacob's sons and all his daughters rose up to comfort him [for the loss of Joseph]. But he refused to be comforted and said: “No, I will go down to the grave mourning for my son.” And his father wept for him. [Gen. 37:35] “His father wept for him” does not refer to Jacob weeping for Joseph, but Isaac weeping because of Jacob's deep pain... So why did Isaac not reveal to Jacob that Joseph was alive? Because Isaac thought: If the Holy One, blessed be He, has not revealed it to him, who am I to reveal it to him? [Genesis Rabbah 84:21]

The Lubavitcher Rebbe [Likutei Sichot 10 p 129ff] adds that Joseph followed the same logic. If God didn't want Jacob to know Joseph was alive, he was not going to inform Jacob either.

Why didn't God want Jacob to know that Joseph was still alive?

Added note: My question, and supporting quotes, is exclusively about God's motives for not wanting Jacob to know -- not Joseph's motives or the brothers' motives, which were addressed elsewhere.

answers.text:
The gemara megilla (end of first perek) says that Yosef was away from Yakov for 22 years as a punishment for Yakov not doing kibud av that same amount of time.

Now why did Yakov have to think he was dead?

  1. So he wouldnt find him.

  2. Perhaps could say like rashi in beginning of vayeshev, that Yakov wanted to take it easy, So God punished Yakov by making him think Yosef wasn't alive.

  3. Also could say Yakov was away from his parents for so long, maybe they thought he was dead. So mida k'neged mida, he thought Yosef was dead.

questions.title_en: Are rabbis infallible?
questions.question:
I am in my first year at a Chabad yeshiva (mostly for convenience, I do not identify as strictly Chabad) and recently, in a debate with my Rabbi, he claimed that rabbis before ~16th century were essentially infallible in not only religious contexts, but also in many secular ones. He gave the example of the Rambam’s medical treatises which, while containing a lot of good wisdom, contains quite a few statements that are verifiably false with today’s medicine. My Rabbi said that despite this, the Rambam could not be wrong, and that perhaps we don’t fully understand the Rambam’s statement or people were simply different back then. He later gave a second example of a colleague of his who disagreed with Ibn Ezra on an issue of dikduk and then stated that Ibn Ezra (and other rabbis) essentially couldn’t be wrong in most fields.

My question is, is the opinion that rabbis are essentially infallible common in the orthodox world or is this merely a Chabad phenomenon. Given the fact that Rishonim and other early rabbis commonly disagreed with each other on hashkafa and other issues, is this “rabbinic infallibility” a recent phenomenon or does it have any real basis?

If a rishon, for example, says that in the times of David Hamelech, everyone had 8 arms, could he be considered wrong?

answers.text:
This answer is based on my experience, take it as you will. First, this is not a Chabad-only position, but the general position of the Ultra-Orthodox ("Chareidim" etc.). Nonetheless, there is nuance to it:

  1. Some hold that they are sometimes fallible, especially in matters that do not directly pertain to Torah*. This will much more likely be an opinion of a more Modern-Orthodox Jew, especially one in the academic/rationalist direction. Even many Ultra-Orthodox will admit this to some degree, given that there are Gemaras that do suggest this themselves, so generally everyone holds they are ultimately human, and thus not perfect like Hashem. How much they think they are fallible is a spectrum.

  2. Some prefer to say it like this: they are indeed human and thus not perfect like Hashem, but nonetheless, we are not on the level to see their fallibility, in the same way a 7 year old who just learned the rules of chess has no way of perceiving any flaw in Magnus Carlsen's chess game (l'havdil). They are so much above us in spiritual and intellectual level, that for all practical purposes, they are perfect to us. If they say something we don't understand, or is seemingly proven wrong, we must find a way to defend them.

  3. There are some that reduce their fallibility to the limit of zero i.e. they are indeed infallible, second only in place to God. This is because they are born with special souls from lofty realms, are indeed speaking with ru'ach hakodesh or minor prophecy, and their teachings are guided by the Hand of Providence. It's important that we do not at all entertain the notion that they are fallible, chas veshalom.

There is wisdom to all 3 approaches and many fine Jews hold by each. The main thing that all Orthodox agree is that we should have a prodigious amount of respect for them, and certainly a huge dose of humility if we ever wish to take on the task of describing them as being wrong about anything.

This is part of "Emunat Chachamim" - faith in our Sages (Pirkei Avot 6:7), and is a very Jewish way of thinking. We don't worship saints, we venerate Sages. We give our respect and trust to our great Torah giants, who have proven themselves worthy of it. It has rarely let us down, and indeed, been one of the pillars of our success as a people, and as transmitters and teachers of the Torah from Sinai to this very day.

* The Lubavitcher Rebbe, I believe, wrote a letter answering how we should deal with the fact that science facts, written by some Rabbis in their Torah teachings, have been proven wrong in modern times. He answers that they were using the science of their time as a "vessel" or "garment" to explain the Torah idea. The fact is, the garment may have changed, but the truth behind the Torah idea is eternal. I've never had any trouble applying this principle

questions.title_en: Bris on Asarah b'Tevet -- how to handle the seudat mitzvah?
questions.question:
When a bris falls out on Asara b'Tevet, what does one do about the Seudat Mitzvah? Is it canceled, does it override the fast, or is it postponed?

Obviously the correct answer here is "Consult your local Orthodox rabbi" (or maybe even "Ask your mohel") but I'm not so much interested in a psak as I am in the question "What are the general principles here, and where can I find this discussed?".

answers.text:
I'm not a posek, ask your LOR

In terms of Psak and sources to learn the sugya more in depth:

The Rema 551:10, Mishnah Berurah O.C 551:76–77, Aruch HaShulchan 551:30, Kaf HaChayim 551:163–165, Chazon Ovadia Arba Taaniyot page. 196, and Teshuvot VeHanhagot volume 5 168:4 pasken that the בעל הברית (father of the child, mohel, and sandak) must fast the entire day on all four fasts (unless it was pushed off until another day, which is a different halacha not for now), and they can have the seudat mitzvah after the fast is over.

Reasoning, General sources and more sources:

I think the reason why this is the psak is based on the following:

Gemera in Shabbat 130a says:

רבן שמעון בן גמליאל אומר: כל מצוה שקיבלו עליהם בשמחה כגון מילה, דכתיב 'שש אנכי על אמרתך כמוצא שלל רב' - עדיין עושין אותה בשמחה

"Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: Any commandment that Israel accepted upon themselves with joy—such as circumcision, as it is written, “I rejoice over Your word like one who finds great spoil”—they still perform it with joy."

Rashi ד״ה בשמחה says that שמחה means making a משתה (meal/seudat mitzvah).

What type of category in halacha is a seudat mitzvah (i.e, deoritah, derabbanan, minhag, etc.)?

The Terumat Hadeshen Siman 269, Shu"t Chavot Yair Siman 70 say that it's a minhag that we do as a celebration for the mitzvah done. Shulchan Aruch Y.D and Rema Siman 265:12 also say that it's a minhag to make a seudat mitzvah for a brit milah known as a seudat mitzvah.

What type of category in halacha are the four fasts (i.e, deoritah, derabbanan, minhag, etc)?

The Ramban in Torat HaAdam and others say that the four fasts were decreed by prophets, and all the stringencies of fasts apply.

Therefore, putting everything together: It seems that the fast pushes off the eating and drinking of the seudat mitzvah for after the fast because the fast comes from the prophets and the seudat mitzvah is a nice minhag that we have, so when they clash, the four fasts push off the seudat mitzvah.

Hope this helps!
My Bris was on a Asara Bteves. Bris was in the morning. My seven year old brother drank the cup of wine (years later still affecting him). Seuda was after Tzeis in the evening.

The translation of מַלְאָךְ as "angel" is coined from Greek for "messenger" not "deputy". Given the many functions of "malakhim", why do Gesenius and JPS1917 render מַלְאָךְ as "angel"?

Reference:

Functions of "angels"

answers.text:
According to Sefer haCarmel which comprises from the etymological commentaries of Malbim, the definition of מלאך is based on commentaries to Isaiah 18:2 and Psalms 103:20:

גדר השם מלאך הוא השליח ההולך בשליחותו נכבדה, דרך כבוד. והוא שליח למי שנישלח אליו בלבד, ואין עליו להחזיר תשובה לשולחיו. והונח על המלאכים שישלחם ה' לעניינים נכבדים או לעשות פלאים ולׂדד הטבע בעת הצורך והגעת הנבואה לנביאים, וכדומה.

The name angel is a messenger who walks in his honorable mission, in a way of honor. He is a messenger to those who sent him only, and he is not required to return an answer to those who send him. It is entrusted to the angels that God sends for honorable matters or to perform miracles and to arrange nature in times of need, and to bring prophecy to the prophets, and the like.

He then goes into discussing angels of G-d. There he notes that a ministering angel (המלאך הממונה) sometimes acts as a messenger without a master. Even in this case the angel is given by G-d a power to perform certain miraculous acts if needed; he is still a messenger without conditions or constraints, and would perform his task as long as he does not get recalled.

questions.question: Does Avuha, as in Avuha D’Shmuel mean father or father of? I’m a bit confused, because father in Aramaic is typically Abba, and if Avuha was “father of”, then isn’t the dalet of D’Shmuel redundant?

answers.text:
Jastrow vowelizes the word as אָבוֹהֵ, meaning "his father".

The form אבוה ד-‏ then literally translates as "his father, of ..." or, more colloquially, "the father of ...". (Compare Hebrew ... אביו של, an example of the so-called "double semikhut" form).

questions.title_en: Are there any limits on using heter mechira or is it just a matter of finding the right rabbi?

questions.title_en: Is microdosing distinct from recreational drug use in halacha?
questions.question:
Microdosing is the ingesting of small enough quantity of a drug that a person does not experience the typical symptoms of "getting high". I understand that the use of recreational drugs, especially psychedelics, may be a matter of halachic disagreement as to whether or not it would violate Devraim 4:15, as interpreted in Berachot 32b and S.A. Choshen Mishpat 427:8. I am curious if there is any halachic discussion on whether or not microdosing would be permitted even according to opinions which would otherwise prohibit usage of such substances.

Why do people Microdose?

As per the linked website. It’s possible that microdosing may help with:

  • Creativity
  • Problem-solving
  • Cognition (thinking skills)
  • Empathy
  • Focus

answers.text: This is a medical question. If a competent doctor says this is evidence-based and actually likely to treat a real problem, with benefits outweighing the costs, then halacha would permit it (assuming no violation of the law of the land). Just like any other medicine that carries risks and side effects. If not, then don't!

questions.title_en: Child-Friendly Financial Literacy Courses
questions.question:
Are there any child-friendly (let's say ages 6 and up, which admittedly is a range of wildly different capabilities) and hashkafically appropriate books or courses that focus on financial literacy?

Just as a starting point, I'll define the terms as I understand them, but would be happy to hear other interpretations as well:

Financial Literacy here is being defined as learning how to properly manage money, i.e. budgeting, saving for retirement, debt management, etc.

The "hashkafic" elements would likely include attitudes relating to earning money (i.e. proper balance of hishtadlus and bitachon) and proper usage of money (i.e. giving tzedakah, less of a focus on gashmius, etc.).

While looking into this, ran into the the following resources:

An organization called Mesila (looks really good)for

Living Smarter Jewish (from the OU. Also looks good, but a bit more limited to High School and above)

The Ramsey kids program (the fact that it has giving as a key point of their curriculum is nice. Not entirely sure how aligned the overall hashkafic ideals are)

The Tuttle Twins (this might be a bit broader than what I'm looking for, it looks more Macro than Micro)

It's very possible one of these is an answer, if anyone has experience with any of them and wants to expand on it, that would work.

answers.text:
There is a book Menachem and Lieba Learn to Budget by Bruchy Laufer. There are also some related episodes on the Marvelous Middos Machine show (around the song "Never take kids to a store"), in fact all 4 episodes are great although they have a much wider focus (1, 2, 3, 4).

There are also some classic Jewish stories coming from novels of Rabbi Marcus Lehmann: "Of Riches and Faith", Wanderings of a Coin, "The Treasurer's Secret"; also Gold's "Settling Accounts", which focus on sacrifices that people made in properly managing money.

Finally, some Jewish high schools offer a Personal Finance course, where they learn basic of managing money; some use a textbook "Foundations in Personal Finance" by RamseyEducation.

Finally, for those who want to have an advanced knowledge of financial markets, one can suggest "The laws of ribbis" by R' Yisroel Reisman, who discusses many complex financial products in the context of las of ribbis. Details of these products can be learned on wikipedia or investopedia.

questions.title_en: Dealing with guilt around anger at the divine
questions.question:
This question has been bottled up for years but AI convinced me to ask if as it needs a human touch.

My mother passed away a few years ago, sort of young and unexpected. People told me to "grieve" but one of the strongest feelings I had was anger at Gd.

She got sick and was first neglected in a rehab center, and then transferred to the hospital during Holiday season (right around now). We all assumed she'd be fine but one day..she wasn't. It feels like the timing was bad (low staff) along with a few mistakes (tried wrong medication etc). It makes me feel like it wouldn't have taken a miracle for her to survive, just a gentle divine nudge.

So I built up this anger about the situation, and at the same time I felt guilty for being angry, since people deal with much worse. I was also scared to be angry because "how dare I" be angry when so many other things go well for me. Stories like Tisha B'Av being retribution for the spies "cries" makes me nervous to "unnecessarily" be upset.

I've never voiced or even wrote this down from fear of manifesting "smite" but honestly I think just want to repair the relationship.

How do I move forward when I'm stuck between needing to express my feelings but being terrified of the consequences.

answers.text:
While Mi Yodeya can't give you personalised advice, here's a story I once heard that is true, and has relevant wisdom:

There was a holocaust survivor, a professor, and he was angry at God and abandoned Judaism. He was living in a community in Eretz Yisrael and there was a Rabbi there who was well known for being well versed in science and philosophy - a genius - and had a popular class on Torah.

Many of his friends would regularly tell him to join the class because he would enjoy it, but he refused. He didn't want to have anything to do with Rabbis or Torah, or God. People also told the Rabbi about the professor, and at some point they actually met - I believe they ended up in an elevator (lift) together.

The Rabbi asked the man to come to class, and the man refused, but they got into a chat anyway and in the end, the professor actually said that he was impressed with what the Rabbi was teaching, and enjoyed it. As they were departing the Rabbi suggested that he join the class, and the professor said no, he can't.

The Rabbi asked why he can't, and he said "you don't understand, you and me, we are not the same - we are completely different. I am angry at God because of the holocaust, I can never forgive Him. I am so angry in fact, that every Friday night, I deliberately make a meal of pork, just to stick it to Him."

The Rabbi said, "not at all! We are exactly the same, we both keep Shabbat!".

They departed and after a couple of weeks, the professor joined the class. When his friends asked him why, he said, "that Rabbi is very smart. Very very smart. Listen to what he was saying. I thought that I was too far 'gone' to have anything to do with Torah, Judaism or God. I was eating pork on Shabbat, in spite and anger. The exact opposite of what a Jew should do, but when the Rabbi made the joke that we are actually the same, there was a big truth in it. Why was I eating pork? Because I knew it angered God. And why was I doing it on Shabbat? Because I knew that Shabbat is a special day to God. In a deep sense, I am a believer, son of believers, I believe in Shabbat, I believe in God, in fact, in my anger, I am in a very close relationship with Him. Therefore, I have no reason to not join this class".

Being angry at God is obviously not ideal (and I'm sure you've read some scary literature on this), but the truth is that some of the people who are angry at Him are in a more real relationship with Him than many believers. What does Hashem want? For us to be in a real relationship with Him, with Emunah.

I can't speak to your situation and I of course recommend speaking to a Rabbi who can get to know you and your specific situation. But I'm sure if you read up on this very topic you'll find a lot of Rabbis have said very reassuring things. We are living in spiritually dark times, and Hashem is very patient and understanding. Above all, He's glad you're still thinking about Him, even if it's in anger. There are many Jews who have completely abandoned Him, and many "religious" Jews who are not as close to Him as you may be.

Try asking yourself -- is the anger/guilt cycle helping you, or holding you back?

By all means acknowledge your feelings, but every so often we get someone here who says, "I feel so guilty about XYZ that I'm not doing mitzvos!" ... which is just making things worst. First focus on what you're actually doing every day.

There's the famous story of the group of rabbis in the early days of the Holocaust that held God on trial ... and concluded He was guilty. And then they got up and davened Mincha.

I heard one therapist comment -- "we can't control our thoughts, but we can control our thinking." So okay. You're feeling angry at G-d. A lot of religious people can have that feeling. You can acknowledge it and then move on, instead of letting it consume you.

questions.title_en: Why does the Shaarei Ephraim recommend against splitting the leining between baalei kriah?
questions.question:
Shaarei Ephraim 3:6 says ideally, all of the leining in one morning should be done by one baal kriah -- even if there are multiple sifrei Torah.

לכתחלה אין לקרות ע"י קורא אחר קורא אפילו אם הקריאה בב' וג' ספרים לא יחלקו לקוראים רק אותו שהתחיל לקרות יגמור לקרוא כל הקרואים שבאותו היום

He points to Birkei Yosef 282, which I'm assuming is OC282:12:

You asked -- if a holiday or New Moon coincides with Shabbos, may the one reciting the Maftir be the same one reading the second Sefer Torah, as there is a break of kaddish between them, or is it prohibited because of a slight to the first reader? Answer: once there is a break of kaddish between them, [the first reader] is like any other member of the community, and it makes no difference if another person gets up to read the second Torah, or he himself does it.

So first off, if the Birkei Yosef allows it in the two-Sefer case, why is the Shaarei Ephraim advising against it?

Furthermore, is that the only reason to avoid dividing the leining between readers, to not slight the first reader? What's the earliest source of this? Would it apply if a shul actually split it 7 ways, in a dina deGemara "you-bench-it-you-lein-it" fashion?

I've certainly seen the very prevalent practice -- puk chazi -- of smaller communities routinely splitting it up, but is that actually defended anywhere?

answers.text: My edition of sharie Efraim corrects the citation to Machzek Beracha, and the Machzek Beracha 282:21 cites from the maharik that there should be a single individual reading the Torah, just like the Torah was given through a single emissary with Moshe Rabenu.

questions.title_he: What is the Original Source for the Name of the Offering מנחת חינוך?
questions.question:
The מילואים process known later to us as a “minchas chinuch” is derived from Vayikra near the beginning of פרשת צו:

(ויקרא ו:יג) זֶה קׇרְבַּן אַהֲרֹן וּבָנָיו אֲשֶׁר יַקְרִיבוּ לַה' בְּיוֹם הִמָּשַׁח אֹתוֹ עֲשִׂירִת הָאֵפָה סֹלֶת מִנְחָה תָּמִיד

From this section, חז"ל learn that when a כהן is about to do עבודה in the מקדש for the first time, he is obligated to bring a special קרבן מנחה which we now know as the מנחת חינוך (seeming to later influence the naming of the famous sefer bearing that name as a play on this korban in conjunction with the focus on the Sefer HaChinuch).

The notion of an actual obligation for כהנים to offer a special separate korban mincha when beginning עבודת המקדש for the first time appears in the following sources. Here the term “chinuch” hasn’t yet been introduced:

תוספתא שקלים ג:טז - כהן הדיוט אין נכנס לעזרה לעבודה אלא א"כ הביא עשירית האיפה משלו ועובדה בידו

ספרא צו פרשה ג:ג - כשהכהן מתקרב תחלה לעבודה מביא עשירית האיפה משלו ועובדה בידו

ברייתא ירושלמי שקלים ז:ג - …..דְּרִבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל אָמַר. עִשָּׁרוֹן מְקַדֵּשׁ. כְּשֶׁהַכֹּהֵן מִתְקָּרֵב תְּחִילָּה לָעֲבוֹדָה מֵבִיא עֲשִׁירִית שֶׁלּוֹ וְעוֹבְדָהּ בְיָדוֹ.

We see the term “חינוך” introduced into this process in the following גמרות:

ירושלמי שקלים ז:ג (המשך) - …..רִבִּי מָנָא בָעֵי מֵימַר. בּוֹ בַיּוֹם נִתְקָרֵב כַּתְּחִילָּה לָעֲבוֹדָה. בּוֹ בַיּוֹם נִתְמַנֶּה לִהְיוֹת כֹּהֵן גָּדוֹל. מֵבִיא שְׁתַּיִם. אַחַת לְחִינּוּכוֹ וְאָחַת לְחוֹבַת הַיּוֹם.

גמ' מנחות עח. - אֶלָּא מַקִּישׁ חִינּוּכוֹ לְהִמָּשְׁחוֹ: מָה הִמָּשְׁחוֹ רְבוּכָה, אַף חִינּוּכוֹ רְבוּכָה. אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא: כֹּהֵן גָּדוֹל הַמִּתְקָרֵב לַעֲבוֹדָה צָרִיךְ שְׁתֵּי עֶשְׂרוֹנוֹת הָאֵיפָה, אַחַת לְהִמָּשְׁחוֹ, וְאַחַת לְחִינּוּכוֹ.

רש"י (מנחות שם) - מקיש חינוכו - דכהן הדיוט להמשחו (היינו רבוכה) וחינוכו הוא המילואים שלו אלמא דבמילואים הוי רבוכה דכהן הדיוט מביא חביתין [היינו רבוכה] ביום חינוכו לעבודה וכהן גדול בכל יום: ואחד לחינוכו - בשביל שנתחנך היום לעבודת כהן [גדול]

Finally, the first time I have seen an appearance of the actual term “מנחת חינוך” is in the Mishna Torah of the Rambam:

הלכות מעשה הקרבנות יב:ד - וְתֵשַׁע מִנְחוֹת הַיָּחִיד וְכֻלָּן קְרֵבִין לַמִּזְבֵּחַ וְאֵלּוּ הֵן. ……הַמִּנְחָה שֶׁמַּקְרִיב כָּל כֹּהֵן תְּחִלָּה כְּשֶׁיִּכָּנֵס לַעֲבוֹדָה שֶׁמַּקְרִיב אוֹתָהּ בְּיָדוֹ וְהִיא הַנִּקְרֵאת מִנְחַת חִנּוּךְ

Is there anyone prior to the Rambam who had coined the term “מנחת חינוך”?

questions.title_en: Why does Rashi say that Yackov said he will only pass away "once", if he never passed away at all?
questions.question:
B"H

Given that Yackov didn't die, even physically and literally, why does Rashi in parshas Yayigash say Yackov said he would pass away "(only) once"?

  1. Then Israel said to Joseph, “Now I can die content, having seen your face and having seen that you are still alive.” לוַיֹּ֧אמֶר יִשְׂרָאֵ֛ל אֶל־יוֹסֵ֖ף אָמ֣וּתָה הַפָּ֑עַם אַֽחֲרֵי֙ רְאוֹתִ֣י אֶת־פָּנֶ֔יךָ כִּ֥י עֽוֹדְךָ֖ חָֽי:

אָמוּתָה הַפָּעַם - (lit.) This time I can die. The straightforward meaning is as Onkelos translates it: אִלּוּ אֲנָא מָאִית זִמְנָא הָדָא מְנַחֵם אֲנָא “If I were to die at this time, I would find comfort.” But its Midrashic explanation is: “I thought I would die twice, in this world and in the World to Come, because the Divine Presence left me and I thought that the Holy One, blessed be He, would demand punishment for your death from me. Now that you are still alive, I will only die once, in this world.” אָמוּתָה הַפָּעַם. פְּשׁוּטוֹ כְתַרְגּוּמוֹ. וּמִדְרָשׁוֹ סָבוּר הָיִיתִי לָמוּת שְׁתֵּי מִיתוֹת, בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה וְלָעוֹלָם הַבָּא, שֶׁנִּסְתַּלְּקָה מִמֶּנִּי שְׁכִינָה, וְהָיִיתִי אוֹמֵר שֶׁיִּתְבָּעֵנִי הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מִיתָתְךָ, עַכְשָׁו שֶׁעוֹדְךָ חַי, לֹא אָמוּת אֶלָּא פַעַם אַחַת

answers.text:
The second death is the death that Yaakov would soon experience.

The first death Yaakov experienced was when Yoseph went missing and Yaakov became too disturbed to experience the Shechinah.

It would seem that Rashi learned that Yaakov thought he was responsible for Yoseph's situation (because he didn't stop Yoseph from being a jerk to his brothers). I have heard elsewhere that Yaakov suspected that Yoseph was alive because he was still aggrieved after he mourned for Yoseph. i.e. the mourning was ineffective because Yoseph was not really dead.

questions.title_en: What is the meaning of the Hebrew markings on the flags in Cremaster 2?
questions.question:
The Cremaster cycle is a series of five loosely connected surrealist art films made between mid 90s to early 00s, filmed by a Matthew Barney, a former medical student and quarterback turned performance artist and sculptor. In Cremaster 2, which is actually the fourth since they were purposely released out of order, there is a scene where a man is marched off to be executed for murder, and someone off screen drops some flags on the ground at his feet. Each include some cryptic symbols seen throughout the series, along with Hebrew markings in thick black letters.

I'm awfully curious about the meanings of the Hebrew inscriptions on these flags and any symbolic significance they might have. As far as I know, Matthew Barney is not Jewish, and this is the only example of the Hebrew language or any other Jewish symbolism appearing int he Cremaster cycle or in any of his other works. I tried asking this on the movies/tv site too, but I figured I might have better luck asking people who actually understand the language and writing system.

answers.text:
They're names of the Twelve Tribes of Israel. Specifically:

  • Ephraim (technically a sub-tribe of Joseph)
  • Issachar
  • Naphtali

questions.title_en: Footnotes on the bottom of the pages of "Doros HaRishonim" by Rabbi Y.Y. Rabinowitz
questions.question:

answers.text: The footnotes are clearly those of an author, not of an editor (same style as main text, additional arguments and ideas rather than editorial work). Only the footnote on the first page is incomplete, and beginning with the parentheses (הערה זו...) is added by the editor. questions.title_en: Halachic Status of Pennies for Tzedakah After the End of Penny Production
questions.question:
With recent news that the U.S. government is discontinuing the production of pennies, I’m a bit confused about how this affects the status of pennies in everyday use and, more specifically, in the context of tzedakah.

From what I understand, no new pennies will be minted, but existing pennies will continue to circulate and are still considered legal tender. However, in practice, many cash transactions may begin rounding totals to the nearest nickel, and some businesses may no longer want to deal with pennies at all.

This raises a question for me regarding tzedakah:

If someone gives charity using pennies — for example, four pennies (4¢) — does this still fully count as a valid act of tzedakah? Or does the fact that pennies are no longer being produced (and may be functionally phased out of daily transactions) affect their halachic or practical status as “real money”?

More specifically:

Since pennies are still recognized by the U.S. government as legal tender, does that alone mean they retain full monetary value for purposes of tzedakah?

If, in everyday commerce, cash totals are rounded and pennies are rarely accepted, does that change whether such a donation is considered meaningful or valid?

From a halachic perspective, is the defining factor the coin’s legal status, its market acceptability, its purchasing power, or the intent of the giver?

Would giving multiple pennies together (e.g., 4¢, 10¢, etc.) be viewed differently than giving a single penny?

Is there any precedent or discussion in halacha regarding currencies or coins that remain legal tender but are no longer produced or commonly used?

I’m asking both from a practical standpoint and a halachic one, and I’d appreciate insight from anyone familiar with Jewish law, monetary policy, or communal charity practices.

answers.text:
The two clarifications I have seen from the Poskim are:

  1. May not contradict Torah law. (this practical application does get a bit complicated)
  2. Must be in accord with the nation's constitution. So if for example a dictator makes some law confiscating property without due process in the USA, we would not need to follow.

questions.title_en: How do we know if Hashem is testing us or giving us a sign?
questions.question:
How can we tell if something is a sign or a test?

Chabad says that "signs" do not exist, that we should always interpret obstacles as a test of our faith, however this is only applied to explicit commands from Him.

Abraham chose to ignore the river—based on the same principle we have been talking about here. When the water reached a point that Abraham and Isaac could not continue without drowning, Abraham called out to G‑d, 'You told me to sacrifice my son. If he drowns, how can I do that?”—and the river disappeared.'"- https://www.chabad.org/library/article_cdo/aid/1274396/jewish/Is-This-a-Sign-or-a-Test.htm#:~:text=The%20“signs”%20we%20see%20that,more%20than%20it%20can%20handle.”

What about signs that enforce the negative mitzvos? For example, if a secular Jew's computer unexpectedly dies at the time that shabbos starts, is that not a sign he should not use his computer? I reject the notion that is coincidence.

All of this brings me to: What if something is more morally grey, and there is no explicit mitzva for or against it. (Or, there are contradicting mitsvos.)

For example, going to shul to daven Mincha when one is sick. Of course it is important to daven Mincha, but there is also the commandment Shmirat HaGuf, telling us to protect our own health and presumably that of others whenever possible. If it is particularly difficult to get to shul that day, is it a sign one should not, or a test and therefore a sign one should/can?

answers.text:
A: If it's preventing you from doing the correct thing it's generally understood to be a test. If there are instances where you are unsure what's correct an therefore you dont know if its a test, best ask your rabbi as circumstances alter the answer significantly.

[For example going to Shul when sick can depend on how sick, what sickness, how detrimental going to Shul is ect.]

B: As far as "signs" go generally the understanding is that we don't interpret "signs" because we aren't privy to God's knowledge and can't fully understand. For example in your case, this time his computer powered down 10 min before shabbos. but next week when his dead computer finally powers on 10 min before shabbos would you say that it's a sign that he should use it on shabbos??

questions.title_en: database/list of jewish names
questions.question:
Is there a database or list I can consult to find an extensive list of “Jewish” names (in the sense that they are recognized as such religiously)?

The inspiration for this question comes from something I remember hearing that Alexander the Great was so favorable toward the Jews that “Alexander” became a Jewish name. What qualifies a name as Jewish, and is there a resource that catalogs them?

answers.text:
סענדער in Yiddish, or סנדר in Hebrew, both "Sender," is the diminutive version of Alexander and are used as Jewish names. It is based on the story of Shimon HaZadik meeting Alexander the Great and agreeing have all the sons of the kohanim born that year named for Alexander rather than to have Alexander's statue erected in the Beit Hamikdash.

במדרש ר' דוד הנגיד מסופר עוד, שאלכסנדר מוקדון ביקש שיקבעו את דמות דיוקנו בבית המקדש. שמעון הצדיק הסביר לו שעל פי התורה יש איסור לעשות פסל וכל תמונה, ובמקום זאת הבטיח לו שכל הילדים שייוולדו לכהנים בשנה ההיא ייקראו בשם אלכסנדר

Shimon Hatzadik took Alexander to the Bais Hamikdash allowing him to enter as far as a gentile could. Alexander requested that they build a statue in his form and place it in front of the Alter. Shimon HaTzadik explained this was not possible for religious reasons but to prove their devotion to him, all cohanim born that year would be named Alexander. It is from this incident that Alexander became a Jewish name. Found in this version at https://www.zissil.com/topics/Shimon-HaTzadik ) and also at https://www.sefaria.org/The_Jewish_Spiritual_Heroes%2C_Volume_I%3B_The_Creators_of_the_Mishna%2C_Simon_the_Just.26?ven=english|The_Jewish_spiritual_heroes,_by_Gershom_Bader._New_York,_N.Y._1940&lang=bi

While there are many lists of Jewish names on-line, like https://aish.com/hebrew-and-jewish-names-for-boys/ and https://www.learnreligions.com/hebrew-names-for-boys-4148288 and https://www.chabad.org/library/article_cdo/aid/3825225/jewish/Popular-Jewish-Hebrew-Boy-Names.htm , I do not know of a "comprehensive" list. Also, what is considered a Jewish name clearly has changed over time. Look at all the Jewish names in the Tanach that are no longer used. Yishmael was an accepted name but now is no longer used; Zerubavel was a Kohen Gadol; Mordechai is based on the 'god' marduk; modern Israeli names were not in use 2 centuries ago and Yiddish names then used may not be common today. This year names like Be'eri and Oz have become common. I do not believe that there is a "religious" basis for accepting a name as "Jewish." Rather that it is based on the custom of the times although some names (eg, Abraham) have long traditions behind them.

Is there a database or list I can consult to find an extensive list of “Jewish” names (in the sense that they are recognized as such religiously)?

It is not all-encompassing but there is a very comprehensive list on the Aish website.

For boys here

For girls here

There are several books published on the subject.

  1. Rabbi Shmuel Gorr Jewish Personal Names. Their Origin, Derivation and Diminutive Forms.

  2. Alexander Beider Dictionary of Ashkenazic Given Names.

  3. Alfred J Kolach The New Name Dictionary

The main sources for Jewish names are Tanach, Gemara, and other Jewish texts. There are some responsa by R. Chaim Kanievsky on names, such as שמות בארץ and אוצר שמות חיים, which cover a small portion.

I could not find research on Sephardic, Bukharean, and other Oriental Jewish given names.

questions.title_en: Why are we not required to relight the shamesh if it goes out before the Hanukka candles?
questions.question:
If the shamesh light is there so we will not inadvertently use the light of the Hanukka candles, why are we not required to relight the shamesh if it goes out before the Hanukka candles?


Source: R Daniel Schloss lecture at Yeshevat HaKotel about 2000

answers.text:
I'm not a posek, please ask your LOR

The Shulchan Aruch O.C. Siman 673:1 says:

ידונוהגים להדליק נר נוסף כדי טושאם ישתמש לאורה יהיה לאור הנוסף שהוא אותו שהודלק אחרון טזויניחנו מרחוק קצת משאר נרות מצוה

"We have the custom to kindle an additional light, in order that if one uses its illumination, it would be the additional light, which was kindled last, and it should be placed at a small distance from the other obligatory lights."

Mishneh Berurah there Seif Katan 14 says:

ונוהגין להדליק נר נוסף - פי' מלבד הנר שמניחין על השולחן דחוששין כיון שמדליקין בפנים אולי ישתמשו בנרות של חנוכה ולאו אדעתייהו אבל מעיקר הדין כיון שיש לו נר על שולחנו א"צ להדליק נר נוסף

“And the custom is to light an additional candle — meaning, aside from the candle that is placed on the table — because there is a concern that since the candles are lit indoors, one might come to use the Chanukkah candles unintentionally and without realizing it. However, halachically speaking, since one already has a candle on his table, there is no need to light an additional candle.”

The Piskei Teshuvot 673:8 explains, based on the Mishneh Berurah, that since nowadays we have electricity where one has the option to have the electric lights on in the same room one lights the Chanukah candles, one doesn't need to light the shamash, however, it has become a widespread minhag, and there are various sources discussing that. I'll add that it's also מנהג ישראל תורה היא to do so as well.

I would say, based on the above, that if you're in a place that has the electric lights on, then you don't need to relight the shamash if it extinguished before the other candles, since the electric lights will stop a person from using the Chanukah lights to do things which is assur (but if a person wants he obviously can). But if the electric lights are not on, then one should relight the shamash in accordance with Shulchan Aruch.

questions.title_en: I Mizrahi on tiruf da'at
questions.question:
Moshe Halevi Spero says on p 207 of his book Judaism and Psychology as follows: "I. M. Mizrahi (18th cent.) permitted eating non-kosher broth to prevent tiruf da'at.”

I have been searching unsuccessfully for this source, also hoping to find there a discussion of וחי בהם (i.e. that mitzvot support life). (Though in fact, Spero gives the context for Mizrachi's ruling as והשבתו לו.) Israel Meir Mizrachi wrote פרי הארץ, which I have accessed in Rashi Script. Though I cannot easily read it, its text is searchable, but nothing comes up for טרוף דעת in that search.

In which source does the Mizrachi refer to טרוף דעת and non-kosher broth?

(Additionally, is פרי הארץ available, either printed or online, in the square Hebrew script, or even in English?)

answers.text:
I believe the relevant piece is to be found in Pri HaAretz vol. III, YD 2. He doesn't use the specific phrase טירוף הדעת (which may be why you were having trouble searching for it) but instead discusses the use of non-kosher chicken broth to treat someone who

יצא מדעתו באופן שיוצא יחידי בלילה ... והוצרכו לאוסרו בכבלי ברזל

was suffering from mental illness to the extent that he would wander alone at nights ... and who they therefore needed to confine using iron chains.

The edition available of this work at HebrewBooks.org is in Rashi script, and also appears to be missing the page containing that question that R. Mizrachi was asked.

There is an edition in square script available on Otzar HaChochmah. You need to have an account in order to access it, but I think that if you do have an account the relevant pages are available for free.

questions.title_en: Is there a source in Jewish teaching for a passage similar to the following
questions.question: Is there a source in Jewish teaching for a passage similar to the following? I have been told that somewhere in the Talmud or elsewhere there is language along the line of this: "If someone tells you that you are inebriated and you don’t think you are, you might ignore it. If a second person tells you that you are inebriated, you begin to wonder. If a third person tells you that you are inebriated, go home and sleep it off." answers.text:
There is no source for this in the Talmud or any similar early Jewish text. It seems to be a modern version of the Chinese Proverb Three Men Make a Tiger.

While this Chinese proverb may be original, the underlying concept could stem from the requirement of two or three witnesses in Deuteronomy 19:15.

Asserting a new technology?*), because I am not interested in that.

I am more interested on the side of asking whether this falls squarely under the laws of "amira l'akum" or if this is not a case of that? And if not, what other issues are relevant?

Is it more akin to asking a Golem to do melacha on Shabbat? What halachic discussions are there on using a Golem in this way (it seems we don't have a question about that on this site).

EDIT: * Here's an example, beyond asserting some new theoretical technology that allows it to listen and compute in a way that doesn't break Shabbat (which almost defeats the question itself): AI is getting better and better at pattern recognition. At some point it will be genuinely clever enough that just by standing around and observing us, it will figure out the majority of melachos that would benefit us at any relevant point - it will just know when we need lights switched, food cooked, pots stirred, clothes cleaned, etc. We won't have to do anything explicit, like talk to or gesture at it, or even think about it! Would it be permissible to have such a Robot in one's house, activated? If not, what exact issues are there?

questions.title_en: Why Attribute Siyum Celebrations to Rav Pappa Rather Than Abaye?
questions.question:
In every tractate in Artscroll's first page of the Hadran, they have a footnote saying something along the lines of:

"In the simple sense, Rav Pappa was a very rich man who, whenever he completed a tractate, used to make great celebrations to which he invited his ten sons, as well as many others. As a result, he brought glory to the Torah, which was reflected in the scholarly attainments of his sons. The nation, therefore, honours Rav Pappa and his family by mentioning them at every siyum." At the end they quote Teshuvos HaRema; Yam Shel Shlomo, Bava Kamma, end of chapter 7).

I have a few difficulties with this explanation:

  1. I have not seen one source in the Gemara that says that Rav Pappa made these celebrations; it just says he was rich!? It was Abaye who used to make a siyum/yoma tava for Rabbis who completed a tractate, as mentioned in Shabbat 118b.
  2. Even if it's a mesorah passed down to us, why wouldn't they include it in the Gemara if it's so important to make a siyum? Yet Abaye’s statement of him making a siyum makes it in!?
  3. If it wasn't passed down as mesorah, how can the Rema assume that just because he’s rich (Pesachim 49a, 113a, 11b in the Rashbam, Bava Metzia 65a with Rashi, Horayot 10b and Rashi) he made a party?
  4. The Rema in Y.D Siman 246:26 himself quotes that we make a siyum on a tractate attributed to Abaye, to make a seudat siyum for anyone who finished a tractate. So why does he quote Abaye in one place and Rav Pappa in another place!

Please include sources. Creative answers are welcome as long as they are backed up; thanks.

questions.title_en: Sheitels (avodah zarah)
questions.question:
I have followed Be'ezrat Hashem (YouTube channel, rov Yaaron Reuven) for quite a while, they're very anti-sheitels because of the claim that sheitels made from real hair are for such and such percentage made out of hair from India.

Now this has been asked before, two times from what I could find, on miyodeya. One from over 10 years ago and another one from a few years ago, none that can satisfy my question.

Are the claims right, that most if not all is from avodah zarah? If so, why would some of the most frum households wear sheitels?

I really want to find out, as I don't want to accuse others of wearing something made from avodah zarah, ChvSh.

answers.text:
Rav Belsky wrote extensively on this issue years ago and presents reason for no prohibition at all. One can read his Hebrew teshuva which is more lengthy than his English Teshuvos (both Shulchan Halevi).

I don't think it is your issue to decide whether someone is doing an issur or not. You should ask your posek and follow that person. Opening bottle caps on shabbos is very halachicly debated ranging from permitted to a full blown Torah violation, and yet I don't see people yelling at each other over it at a shabbos meal. There will always be debate in halacha from reputable poskim.

questions.title_en: Seeking Honour L'shem Shamayim - how can one pursue teaching Torah without "seeking honour"
questions.question:
People are much more likely to properly listen to and absorb from people they respect. They are much more likely to ignore people they do not respect. This is a given.

It seems like we should be averse to honour, and many stories and aggada drill that home, including the famous "those who chase greatness will have it flee from them, those who run away from it will be pursued by it" (Eruvin 13b), and "do not seek greatness for yourself, and do not covet honour" (Avot 6:5)

However, it seems that if one truly does know the truth, and has wisdom to teach it and influence others for good, honour would be an extremely important tool. People listen to those who they respect, and ignore those who they don't. Therefore, a true Talmid Chacham should hope for honour, purely l'shem shamayim! So he can teach Torah!

I would say that there is nowhere in Torah that teaches that we should seek honour l'shem shamayim. Am I being ignorant? If so, please bring me sources that do explain this (it would indeed go well with the second half of the proverb in Eruvin, as why else would it bother to tell us how honour is achieved, if we are meant to only avoid it?)*

If I am right, and this is against the Torah, why? What's wrong with my argument? Is it that we should always leave honour to Hashem's Hashgacha? Is it that honour is so bad for our soul that there's no viable way to "seek" or "pray for" it? Is it that honour is reserved for Olam Haba and it's not relevant to this life at all - even the fact that it would help a Talmid Chacham influence people for good is not important enough to make honour something for Olam Hazeh? Is it simply that seeking honour, and "l'shem shamayim" are oxymorons?

Either way, l'ma'aseh, what should someone knowledgable in Torah, with a desire to teach, do? Practically? If he must hate honour and take no steps to gain people's respect, does that equate to him quenching his mission (and desire) to teach? Should he aim to teach a tiny, irrelevant class that nobody attends, perhaps even actively lying to people about how knowledgable he is (and definitely not doing this while secretly hoping people will come to respect him and his Torah anyway)? If not, then how can one pursue teaching Torah without "seeking honour"?

* some might claim that the answer is that it's ok to seek honour for Torah, and therefore if one learns a lot of Torah, he can expect and even demand a lot of honour for said Torah that is in him. I'm not sure that that will be a truly satisfying answer. Not everyone who knows a lot is good at communicating it, for example, and it's still going to involve some level of seeking personal honour - it just has to. People have to honour you first, before they can find out that you are filled with honourable Torah! As I said, people only really listen to people they already respect...

questions.title_en: Believers sons of believers - how is lack of belief explained?
questions.question:
There is a principle that the Jewish soul inherits an automatic belief in Hashem from the Patriarchs such that we are "believers, sons of believers" (Shabbat 94a)

There are some, such as Chassidim, who hold by this principle literally, and also very strongly - every Jew, from birth, believes in Hashem, e.g. as the Mittler Rebbe writes in part 3 of ענין ברכת חתנים (דרושי חתונה א):

לא יתכן על האמונה [ציווי] כלל כי האמונה היא בבחי׳ עצמיות וטבעיות בכל א׳ מישראל מיד שיבוא לכלל דעת קצת מאמין בה׳ אמונה חזקה ונפלאה עד שתהא כמו טבע בנפשו ואין צריך לימוד וראי׳ לזה כלל שהרי הנשים וקטנים שם שמים שגור בפיהם באמונה חזקה מאד בלי הקדם לימוד מאביהם בזה כלל וידוע שרש זה [הוא] לפי שהאמונה היא ירושה בכל נפש מישראל מהאבות וכמ״ש מה יפה ירושתינו כו׳ ואברהם אבינו ע״ה אחד הי׳ המאמין הראשון כמ״ש והאמין בה׳ כו׳ וישראל נק׳ מאמינים בני מאמינים עד שהקטן מיד שיגדיל בדעת קצת יאמין כמו הגדול בדעת ממש כידוע

...it is not possible at all that there be a command concerning emunah, for emunah is in an aspect of essentiality and naturalness in every single Jew. As soon as he comes to a little awareness, he believes in God with a strong and wondrous emunah, until it is like a nature in his soul, and it requires no study. And this has no need of proof at all, for women and children have the Name of Heaven fluent in their mouths with very strong emunah, without any prior instruction from their father in this at all.

And it is known that the root of this is that emunah is an inheritance in every Jewish soul from the Patriarchs, as it is said: “How beautiful is our inheritance…”. And Avraham our father, peace be upon him, was the first believer, as it is written: “And he believed in Hashem,” and Israel are called “believers, the children of believers,” to the point that even a small child, as soon as he increases a little in awareness, believes just as a great one in awareness, literally, as is known.

I would like to ask, for those that hold this point of view, how exactly do they explain what's going on with regards to Jews who say and/or feel that they do not believe?

[I am not looking for people to disprove this point of view or argue from a different point of view - EDIT: and it should go without saying, but I am not asking this as some kind of kasha or gotcha, chas veshalom. This is purely a sourced based explanation, which I am sure must exist and I am sure is good and satisfying. Can someone provide it? I strongly suspect it has something to do with mesirat nefesh]

answers.text:
Rav Kook, in his essay Kirvas Elokim (published in Maamarei Haraayah, p. 32) discusses this exact idea. He says that the desire to be close to Hashem exists in every soul, not just Jewish ones. (The principle of "maaminim bnei maaminim" would, in this case, just refer to a greater degree of awareness as a result of the higher level of neshamah that a Jew possesses.) He says that this can be seen through a historical examination of societies, all of whom have pursued a relationship with any sort of deity, be it Hashem or otherwise; and he says that in today's generation, it becomes covered up by all sorts of -isms but it can never be eliminated completely:

ואחרי המשך של בחינות שונות בחזיונות החיים לכל מצביהם ואפניהם נוכח עוד, שכל רובי הצפריעים והמתנגדים לה, שנולדו על ידי הסתבכות החיים החומריים והרוחניים, יוכלו רק למעט לאיזה משך זמן את התגלותה ואת שלטונה על תהלוכות המעשה והמחשבה של האדם, אבל בשום אפן לא לבטלה, לכבשה ולעצרה לגמרי.

And after continuing to examine various visions of life in all its states and aspects, it is further evident that all the many critics and opponents of [a relationship with Hashem], born of the entanglement of material and spiritual life, will only be able to delay its manifestation and its rule over the processions of human action and thought for a certain period of time, but in no way to abolish it, conquer it, and arrest it completely.

Rebbe Nachman discusses this concept as well, in Likutei Moharan Torah 282, where he says that every Jew has a "nekudah tovah" buried deep inside and we are required to see it - even, as the commentaries point out, that nekudah tovah is just being Jewish. He discusses a similar idea in Torah 56, where he talks about the concept of "hastarah shebetoch hahastarah," saying that a Jew doesn't even know how far he is from Hashem. We can correlate this with a lack of belief. When we put those two concepts together, we have a Jew possessing a spark inside of him which can never be extinguished and which may be so covered up or far from Hashem that the Jew himself doesn't realize - but he's still connected, and with enough effort that spark will be revealed.

questions.title_he: תשוקה העצמית - is this term used anywhere else?
questions.question:
In ר״ה, רנ״ז, the Rebbe Rashab uses the term "תשוקה העצמית" to describe Hashem's desire for a dira betachtonim, a dwelling among the lowest beings/in the lowest world:

ופי׳ שנשתוקק הקב״ה לבראותו הוא שיש בזה תשוקה העצמית דא״ס ב״ה, דזה הי׳ תחלת הכוונה שיומשך ויתגלה בעולם למטה בחי׳ התשוקה העצמית דא״ס שהוא בחי׳ שעשועי המלך בעצמותו כו׳, ונמצא דמה שארז״ל שנשתוקק הקב״ה לבראותו הוא ענין א׳ עם מה שאמרו שנתאווה הקב״ה להיות לו דירה בתחתונים, דענין דירה בתחתונים מורה על המשכה עצמית וכמו עד״מ אדם הדר בתוך הבית הרי כל עצמותו הוא בתוך הבית כמו״כ הו״ע דירה בתחתונים דבחי׳ עצמיות א״ס ב״ה יומשך למטה כו׳

And the explanation of “He longed” is that the Holy One, blessed be He, longed to create it, meaning there is in this the essential need/desire of Ein Sof, blessed be He. For this was the beginning of the intention: that in the world below should be drawn forth and revealed the aspect of the essential need/desire of Ein Sof, which is the aspect of the King’s delight in His essence, etc. Thus, what our Sages said, that the Holy One, blessed be He, longed to create it, is the same matter as what they said, that the Holy One, blessed be He, desired [nit’aveh] to have a dwelling place in the lower realms. For the idea of a dwelling place in the lower realms indicates an essential drawing forth. Just as, by way of analogy, when a man dwells in his house, all his essence is within the house, so too the concept of a dwelling place in the lower realms is that the aspect of the Essence of Ein Sof, blessed be He, be drawn below, etc.

The word תְּשׁוּקָה, used to describe a wife's longing and emotional need for her husband (Bereshit 3:16, and a husband's need for his wife - see Yoma 75a), as well as Hashem's longing and need for Yisrael (Shir HaShirim 7:11), is a very enigmatic word. Used only 3 times in the whole Tanach, it is perhaps one of, if not the most romantic and loving words there is between two lovers (interestingly, it is also used to describe the yeitzer hara's longing for us! See Bereshit 4:7).

How much more powerful is the phrase "תשוקה העצמית"! Essential need, arising from the very core of one's self, one's identity.

I have done a lot of searching and I can't find this term used anywhere else. It is beautiful, and I would like to know if this is a wonderful innovation of the Rebbe Rashab, or if he is transmitting it from an older source. Perhaps others here have more access/better search engines than me so please let me know if you find this term anywhere else, used this way.

questions.title_en: How does the halacha view a first born male's double portion inheritance rights in absence of a halachic will today?
questions.question:
Bamidbar 21:17 is the source that a first born male son receives a double portion of inheritance. This is established halachically in Shulchan Aruch, Choshen Mishpat 281. I am aware of a machloket among 20th century poskim including Rav Moshe Feinstein, Rav Shlomo Zalman Aurbach, and the Chazon Ish regarding whether or not, in the absence of a halachic will, but in the presence of a secular will which is different than what the torah prescribes, a first born male would received a double portion.

I am not aware of any published responsa from 21st century poskim (Ashkenazi, Sepharadi, Hasidish or otherwise) who take a stance on this issue other than to align previous poskim.

I would like to know if there are any published teshuvot, or lectures/podcasts from poskim today which deal with a situation wherein a first born male son stands to inherit, there is no halachic will, but there is a secular will which does not give the son a double portion.

questions.title_en: What is the difference between a "light mitzvah" and a "serious mitzvah"?
questions.question:
HaRambam says in the commentary on the Mishnah:

אח"כ אמר שצריך ליזהר במצוה שיחשב בה שהיא קלה כשמחת הרגל ולמידת לשון הקדש כמצוה שהתבאר לך חומרתה שהיא גדולה כמילה וציצית ושחיטת הפסח

Does he ever define a "light" mitzvah and a "heavy"/"serious" mitzvah? Is there a standard way to understand this distinction?

answers.text:
He doesn't say in what you quoted that there are 'light' and 'serious' mitzvos. The translation of what you quoted is

… that one must be as careful with a mitzva he thinks of as light… as with a mitzva whose seriousness is clear to you…

That is, as far as he states in this passage, all miztvos may be equally 'light' or 'serious' and the difference between them is only in how they appear to us. (For which, obviously, every one of us is different.)

questions.title_en: Kohen / Rabbi + “Gentile marriage”: must the answer be simply yes/no? What is the halakhic framing?
questions.question:
I’m asking a halakhic framing question, not seeking personal counselling.

Scenario: In a public setting, a Jewish mother refers to a gentile woman as “my daughter / my child,” and the son refers to the same woman as “my girl … we are one.”

Question:

  1. Is this language halakhically meaningful (status/kinship), or only social speech with no halakhic weight?
  2. If it is only social speech, are there any prohibitions or concerns (mar’it ayin, geneivat da’at, etc.) in presenting it publicly?
  3. What would be the most precise yes/no boundary for what is permitted in public speech vs covenantal status?

(Full text context is available via my profile / references if needed.)

questions.title_he: מדוע בחו"ל לא עושים יו"ט שני ביוה"כ
questions.question: במה שונה יום כיפור משאר המועדים, שבכל המועדים בחו"ל נוהגים ב' ימים של יו"ט ויום כיפור נוהג רק יום אחד? תשובה ביום הכיפורים לא תיקנו חכמים לעשות ב' ימים טובים מפני שיש חשש שיבואו לידי סכנה, והיא גזירה שאין רוב הציבור יכולים לעמוד בה, (שאילות דרב אחאי מו, מאירי ר"ה כא,א וריטב"א ר"ה יח,א). אמנם …

שלום רב,
מספר שאלות ליום הכיפורים.
סליחות –
1) האם יש לבקש סליחה מחבר חילוני (בזמנו גם אני הייתי…) אחרי שניתקתי איתו קשר בצורה חדה וחד משמעית? ידוע לי שנפגע אך בזמנו חשתי כי אין לי ברירה, ושכל דבר שאני מלמד אותו אודות הנפש, הוא משתמש לפגוע ולנצל אנשים ונשים, ואף עשה מעשה כנגדי ומאחורי גבי בשקר גמור. הפסקתי לענות לטלפונים שלו. כיום לאחר כל השנים אני מרגיש שמחלתי לו. היה נוהג הוא לשלוח לי כל חג, חג שמח ולימי שמחה וכו' ולא הייתי משיב. הוא היה חבר יקר בסופו של דבר אך יש חשש שהדבר רק יעורר תרעומות לאחר כל השנים.
2) האם לבקש סליחה מחילונים שזה בשטח אפור? דהיינו, לא עשיתי להם שום דבר משמעותי, אבל אולי פה ושם לא התנהגתי כראוי כפי שנכשל כל אדם. גם כאן מפחד אני שיאמרו שזה משום שחזרתי בתשובה, ועל כן סליחתי אינה כנה, ושהדבר יוביל לחילול שמיים.
3) האם לבקש סליחה מגויים אוהבי ישראל או שלא שייך עניין גויים ליום כיפור?
4) האם לבקש סליחה מנשים שאולי ופגעתי שלא בכוונה לפני שנישאתי? לפני כשנתיים שאלתי רב, והוא אמר שאם אני מוכרח אז רק במייל בשפה רשמית מבלי להיכנס לפרטים ספציפיים. ולבסוף לא כתבתי להן. אך כיום אני "במקום אחר" מבחינת שמירת המצוות כמו שאומרים, ונראה לי העניין לא שייך, אך אני מפחד שיקפידו עליי ח"ו.
5) אם אני מוחל למישהו שהקפדתי עליו, עליי להודיע לו על-כך?
6) חברים שאני לא חש צורך אמיתי לבקש מהם סליחה, האם ראוי שאודיע להם על מעלותיהם?
7) האם יש לבקש סליחה מחילונים שעלולים לנצל זאת כנגדך, אפילו אם הם קרובים? למשל בן דוד שעלול לראות בזה 'מודה במקצת'.

שלום רב,
1. בהחלט אני כלל לא בטוח שהתנהגותך היתה ראויה, ומאד מתאים שתבקש ממנו מחילה עם איזה מכתב יפה.
2. ממש לא אפור, אם אתה סבור שפגעת בהם, ראוי לבקש מהם מחילה.
3. לא שייך ליום כיפור.
4. אני סבור שאתה יכול לשלוח להם מייל כפי שאמר לך וזה בסדר גמור.
5. לא. אינך צריך להודיע.
6. אתה לא צריך לבקש סליחה. אבל מדי פעם אתה בהחלט יכול לפרגן להם, זה יעזור להם – זה ניתן לומר בבטחה, וגם יכול לעזור למעלותיך – ללמוד לפגן לשני זו מעלה גדולה.
7. לא הבנתי מדוע יש בזה מודה במקצת. אם פגעת בו או אם הוא סבור שיש לו תרעומת עליך, מדוע לא לבקש ממנו מחילה, לא צריך להתרפס ולהודות במה שלא היה..

questions.title_he: ישיבה בין שתי נשים שאחת מהן אשתו / איפור קבוע להסתר קעקוע
questions.question:
1. האם יש עניין לא לשבת בין 2 נשים כאשר האחת היא אמא שלי והשנייה היא אשתי? 2. אדם שחזר בתשובה ורוצה לעשות על הקעקוע שלו איפור קבוע בצבע גוף. האם זה מותר?

שלום וברכה,
על עצם הדיון אם הזהירות שלא לעבור בין שתי נשים היא גם בין בני משפחה, בס' שמירת הגוף והנפש ח"א עמ' שלג הביא מס' בית ברוך שמסופק בדבר. ונראה שבישיבה הקלו יותר.
לגבי איפור קבוע לא כל כך פשוט להיתר, אבל כשיש בושה וכדומה יש לעל מה לסמוך להתיר. לצורך קוסמטיקה בלבד אין לעשות איפור קבוע, כיון שיתכן שהדבר אסור מן התורה ולכמה דיעות מדרבנן, אולם אין צורך להוריד את האיפור אם כבר נעשה. במקום צורך כגון תיקון צלקת, המיקל יש לו על מי לסמוך, אבל זה רק בשעת הדחק.
מקורות:
עי’ פסקי דין רבנים ירושלים (כרך ד עמ’ קנג), בדברי הרב ברוך שרגא, ונדפס כמאמר “איפור וכתובת קעקע”, תחומין יח (תשנ”ח), עמ´ 110-114, שהביא בזה את דיעות הפוסקים, אולם הראשל”צ הגר”ע זצ”ל הגם שבתחילה נטה קו לאסור לגמרי אולם לאחרונה חזר בו ופירסם תשובה ארוכה ומפורטת בספרו טהרת הבית חלק ג, ובו כתב שלצורך קוסמטיקה יש להחמיר לכתחילה והמיקל יש לו על מי לסמוך, ולצורך גדול כצלקת וכד’ יש להתיר לכתחילה.

שלום כבוד הרב אדם שמחמיר על עצמו ביום שבת ולא מטלטל כי לא סומך על העירוב האם יכול לטלטל ביום כיפור שלא חל בשבת ?האם דינו כיו"ט או לא? תודה

שלום וברכה
יום כיפור לענין זה דינו כשבת. מה שהוצרה הוצאה ביום טוב הוא בגלל שיש היתר בעשיית מלאכה לצורך אוכל נפש, ומתוך שהותרה לצורך הותרה שלא לצורך כשיש צורך קצת, אבל ביום כיפור שהוא שבת שבתון ולא שייך בו דין זה – דינו כשבת.

שלום וברכה, מה הדין אם יש ילדה למעלה מגיל תשע שרוצים לצום את כל הצום, האם יש להתיר להם? (כעת לא מצאתי זאת מפורש בפוסקים, מלבד בשו"ת חקרי לב ראיתי שמתיר בזה). בתודה רבה

אין להתיר להם, זה מסוכן ומיותר. ילד יצום מקסימום עד חצות היום, ובגיל כזה צעיר גם זה לא. מגיל 12 אם רוצה לצום כל היום זה אפשרי גם לבנים, בנות חייבות מגיל 12.

questions.title_he: בחול המועד האם מותר לחבר דלת לארון
questions.question:
על ידי הברגהתודה

כיון שזה מעשה הדיוט לצורך המועד יש להקל.
מועדים לשמחה.

בס"דשלום רב , שבוע טוב !1. ביום הכיפורים , לאחר ביקור בבית שימוש , וכן לפני כל אחת מהתפילות יש ליטול ידיים עם נטלה 3 פעמים לסירוגין כרגיל ?למטרת טהרה ולא למטרת עונג.והאם מותר להשתמש בקצת סבון נוזלי למי שהתלכלך בבית שימוש ?2. בחורה אשכנזיה שמתפללת לבד בבית ביום הכיפורים , חייבת בכל 5 התפילות ? והאם דיי לומר רק את תפילת העמידה של ה 7 ברכות או יש להתפלל את כל התפילה המלאה ?3. במוצאי יום הכיפורים אחרי רבינו תם , לפני תפילת ערבית מותר כבר לשטוף את הפה ואת הידיים או יש לומר תחילה " ברוך המבדיל" ואז לשטוף ?4. במוצאי יום הכיפורים , אין לומר את הפסוקים שלפני ההבדלה " הנה קל ישועתי " ? ומברכים הגפן , מאורי האש והמבדיל ?5. את נר ההבדלה מדליקים מנר הנשמה ששבת , לפני שאוחזים בכוס ההבדלה ?6. אם חלילה נר הנשמה נכבה קודם זמן ההבדלה , מה עושים ? מדליקים חדש כמו במוצאי שבת או לא מברכים מאורי האש ?7. אם אני לא רוצה לאכול לחם בסעודת הבוקר ובסעודה מפסקת , אפשר עדיין לומר את " לשם יחוד " שלפני הסעודות ?8. להגיד "כל נדרי " אחרי שאני מדליקה את הנרות ?9. יש לברך " להדליק נר של יום הכיפורים " או " נר של יום טוב " ?
אשמח לתשובה מהירה לפני כניסת יום הכיפורים.גמר חתימה טובה !

1. נוטלים פעם אחת, רק בבוקר שלוש פעמים, לפני תפילה אין ליטול רק אחרי שירותים. מותר מעט סבון אם יש בו צורך לניקוי ליכלוך ממשי, יש להזהר לא להתלכלך.
2. ביום כיפור אין לוותר על חמשת התפילות אבל בלי חזרת הש"ץ כמובן.
3. קודם ברוך המבדיל.
4. נכון.
5. או באמצע איך שרוצים.
6. לא מברכים אלא על נר ששבת.
7. אפשר.
8. יחיד לא אומר כל נדרי.
9. של יום הכיפורים.
גמר חתימה טובה.

חיבוט ערבות – האם נשים צריכות לחבוט בערבות בהושענא רבה? האם חייבים דווקא 5? או שאפשר פחות

נהגו שגם נשים וקטנים חובטים ערבות ביום הושענא רבה, משום שכל דבר שיש בו סגולה כמו כפרות או ערבות לא חילקו בו בין אנשים לאנשים, על פי האר"י והרעיון על פי קבלה הטמון בענין זה, חובטים דוקא חמש ערבות כנגד חמש גבורות.

במקום עבודתי מוכרים תרופות טבעיות, אני לא יודעת את הכשרות לפסח, מותר לעבוד שם בחול המועד?

יש להקל.
עצם העבודה בחול המועד מותרת רק אם זה דבר האבד, כלומר חשש פיטורין או כעס גדול מהבוס וכדומה..
חג שמח

האם מותר לי לקחת תרופה בצום? ומה ביום הכיפורים?מדובר בתרופה שצריך לקחת אותה כל יום כחלק מסדרה שלמה של תרופות – לחיידק הליקובקטור. תודה רבה.

שלום וברכה
באופן עקרוני תרופה מסוג זה אין חובה לקחת ביום כיפור, ניתן לקחת מיד לפני הצום ומיד לאחריו, במידה ויש צורך על פי הנחיות הרופא ואי אפשר לדלג, יש לקחת ללא מים. במקרה וגם זה בלתי אפשרי ויש צורך לקחת, ניתן לפגום מים עם קצת מלח ולבלוע עם מעט מאוד, פחות מכשיעור.
רפואה שלמה.

שלום
סוכה העשויה ממסגרת ברזל, ומחיצות בד.מה הסיבה שבכ"ז יש לעשות מחיצות לבוד?באלו מקרים מחיצות הבד כשרות לכתחילה ומתי זה בעייתי ומצריך גם עשיית לבוד?ובעשיית לבוד, האם משנה מה רוחב או עובי החוט או גם חוט דק בסדר?והאם חוט כל סוג שהוא, כולל חוט ברזל?כמה המרחק צריך להיות בין החוטים? ואם זה לא מדויק?ולאיזה גובה בס"ה זה צריך להגיע עם החוט העליון?והאם המדידה היא מהרצפה או מהמסגרת התחתונה?
תודה

הבעיה בבד הוא שזה נע ברוח, ודופן שנעה ברוח מתבטלת ואינה דופן, לכן עושים לבוד, חוטים מהודקים. דעתו של החזון איש בסי’ עז, שאם המחיצה אינה מתבטלת על ידי הרוח לגמרי עד שהדפנות מתרחקות ג’ טפחים היא כשרה, וכן כתב המאירי: צריך שיהא הלחי יכול לעמוד וכן הדין בכל מחיצה הא כל שהרוח באה ועוקרתו לשעתו אינה מחיצה. אולם יש שחולקים ולכן לכתחילה יש לקשור את המחיצות היטב מכל צד שלא ינועו ברוח. וראה עוד כאן בהרחבה מה הטוב יותר לעשות.
יש לעשות חוט כל 20 ס"מ מהודק היטב, לא משנה עוביו אבל שיהיה חזק ולא יוכל להקרע, ושיגיע עד מטר, להרויח שיטת החזון איש שעשרה טפחים זה מטר.
חג שמח.

שלום רב! הכיצד ניתן לומר בשיר היחוד (ליום ראשון) 'ואנחנו על אדמה טמאה'? הרי יושבי ארץ הקודש אנחנו, האין זו כפיות טובה להגיד כך כיום?

בארץ ישראל אין לומר תיבות אלו, כמובן.
חג שמח.

שלום וברכה.הזמנתי רכב חדש לפני כשמונה חדשים, הרכב ההי אמור להמסר כבר לפני שלשה חדשים ויותר,בגלל מגבלות הקורונה העניין התעכב,כעת הגיע הרכב לארץ אלא שנאמר לי שהמסירה בפועל תצא בימי חול המועד, השאלה היא אם ראוי לבקש לדחות את העניין לאחר חול המועד שלא יהא בדבר חשש ביזוי המועדות חלילה, או שמא אין חשש בדבר.יישר כח.

לכאורה קבלת הרכב היא השלמה של הרכישה, והיא גם כרוכה בחתימות וכו', וכיון שמן הסתם אין בזה צורך המועד, שכן יש לך עדיין מן הסתם את הרכב הישן, הייתי דוחה את זה לאחר החג.
נסיעות טובות ונעימות.

questions.title_he: אויר 3 טפחים בסוכה לאורך או לרוחב?
questions.question:
פסול אויר 3 טפחים זה לאורך או לרוחב שבדקתי בסוכה יש אויר טפחים וחצי לרוחב , אבל לאורך זה יותר מדי טפחים , אז איך מודדים ומשערים לפי האורך או הרוחב

הכוונה שרוחב האויר הוא שלושה טפחים, האורך לא משנה, ובלבד שלא יחצה את הסוכה כולה ברצף. אם זה חוצה הכל ברצף תישב איזה קנה לרוחב הסוכה שיחתוך את זה.
מועדים לשמחה.

שלום לרב,בכוונתי לבנות סוכה ולסכך אותה בקני במבוק גסים שיעודם המקורי הוא לשם גדר ולא למחצלת.האם מותר לסכך בהם ואם כן האם חובה לפרום את חוט המתכת שאוגד את הקנים?(הקנים ישבו בגג הסוכה בתוך מגרעת בעץ והוא המעמיד שלהם ולא החוט)בתודה וברכה

שלום וברכה
לא צריך שהיעוד יהיה סכך, העיקר שלא יהיה לשכיבה שאז הוא נחשב דבר המקבל טומאה.
הבעיה היא שמה שכתבת שזה יושב במגרעת אינני בטוח שזה יספיק, הם מאוד קלים ועדיין נראה לי שאם אינם קשורים הם לא יעמדו ועדיין הברזל כאן הוא מעמיד. אם תוציא את החוט זה כמובן בסדר אבל זה יקלקל את המחצלת וחבל קצת… אני הייתי קונה מחצלת עם חוטי גווה כרגיל.
בהצלחה

שלום הרב רציתי לדעת עד איפה צריך לוי ליטול ידיו לפני ברכת כהנים ביום הכפורים?

הלוי אינו נוטל ידיו ביום הכיפורים, רק הלויים נוטלים לכהנים ועל כל היד כרגיל.

שלום הרב, רציתי לדעת אם אני יכול לקבוע שיעור מוזיקה בחול המועד.

אין לקבוע שיעור מוזיקה בחול המועד כיון שהמורה אינו רשאי ללמד בשכר בימי החג.
כמו כן באם לך אין הנאה מכך רק לימוד מפרך, זו מלאכה האסורה במועד.

questions.title_he: תספורת בחול המועד ובספירת העומר לאחר אבלות שלושים
questions.question:
האם מותר לי להסתפר היום לכבוד החג, אתמול סיימתי 31 ימי אבלות,

שלום וברכה
בודאי אסור ומשתי סיבות ואסביר.
ראשית, אבלות השלושים שלך כבר הסתיימו בערב החג, החג הרי מבטל אבלות שלושים, ולכן למשל גזיזת ציפורניים שאסורה כל שלושים היתה מותרת לך כבר בערב החג, וממילא אין סיבה להתיר מלאכות בחול המועד.
שנית, באבלות על הורים אין להתיר תספורת עד שיגיע זמן שיגערו בו חבריו, ולא די בסיום השלושים, וגם מסיבה זו אין להתיר בחול המועד. השאלה מה קורה כשיגיע הזמן שיגערו בו חבריו [שלאשכנזים הוא שלושה חודשים מתספורת אחרונה, ולספרדים עכ"פ שיגערו בו לאחר השלושים ויהיה מגודל], והימים הם ימי ספירת העומר האסורים בתספורת, בענין זה נחלקו הדעות, יש שהקלו לגלח בספירת העומר כיון שלא יכול היה לגלח קודם, והמיקל יש לו על מה לסמוך, ראה סי’ תצג בשערי תשובה ס”ק ג’ שהביא את החיד”א בשם הזרע אמת, שהקל בזה. אמנם בשו”ת נאמן שמואל סי’ מא נראה שהחמיר, אבל לדינא המיקל יש לו ל מי לסמוך. יש לזכור שבאבלות על הורים סיום השלושים מתיר רק את גילוח הזקן, שיעור גערה [לבני אשכנז] בשיער הראש או בסידור זקן קיים, הוא יותר מכך.

questions.title_he: יום טוב שני – בן ארץ ישראל בחו"ל
questions.question:
רווק שנוסע לחו'ל, כיצד ינהג ביום השני, לתפילות קידוש, ומלאכה.
לדעת אשכנז וספרד.
ואם זה נשוי שטס עם אשתו, רק לכמה ימים, האם הדין שונה?

בן ארץ ישראל הנמצא בחו"ל ביום טוב שני ודעתו לחזור לארץ ישראל אחרי כמה ימים, אסור בעשיית מלאכה אפילו בצנעה ואפילו מלאכות דרבנן, אבל הוא מתפלל תפילות של חול, וחייב בהנחת תפילין בצנעה בחדרו. אינו עושה קידוש אלא שומע מבן המקום. ראה שו"ע סי' תצו וס' יום טוב שני כהלכתו פרק ג כל הפרטים בענין זה.
חג שמח.

questions.title_he: ניקוי משקפיים בתשעה באב וביום כיפור, מותר?
questions.question:
שלום כבוד הרב.
האם מותר לנקות משקפיים בט' באב וביום הכיפורים?
תודה מראש.בשורות טובות, ישועות ונחמות.

מותר לנקות את המשקפיים בתשעה באב, אין בזה כיבוס, הזכוכית אינה בגד ולא בולעת, ודינם כמו כל כלי שאנחנו רוצים לרחוץ.
בשורות טובות.

3 שאלות בנושא דופן עקומה. שולחן ערוך, אורך חיים, תרל"ב, א'.יהודי בנה סוכה במרפסת צמוד לביתו. גג הבית, בולט מעל הסוכה הזאת.כך שבפועל יש שטח בסכך הסוכה, בצורת מלבן, שמעליו יש גג.השאלות:1] האם רואים את דופן הסוכה,כאילו היא דופן עקומה ומגיעה עד תחילת הסכך שאין מעליו גג.אבל אסור לאכול ולשתות ולישון תחת לסכך שיש מעליו גג?2] מה מידות אורך ורוחב של המלבן הזה שבהן ההיתר של דופן עקומה תקף,והסוכה אינה נפסלת משום ריחוק הסכך הכשר מ-1 או יותר מדפנות הסוכה.האם זה רק כל עוד הגג בצורת המלבן, קטן מ-4 אמות באורכו, וגם קטן מ-4 אמות ברוחבו?כאשר 1 אמה = 6 טפחים.3] ובאותו נושא, אבל מקרה שונה, האם מותר שכל 1 מדפנות הסוכה תהא דופן עקומה, כל עוד יש בסוכה מספיק סכך כשר?תודה.

שלום וברכה
1. נכון.
2. האורך אינו רלוונטי, העיקר שהרוחב – הריחוק בין הדופן לסכך, אינו יותר מארבע אמות.
3. אפשר גם מכמה צדדים. הדיון המעניין הוא, כאשר אני צריך את הדופן עקומה לא מחמת סכך פסול מעליה, אלא מחמת שהיא גבוהה למעלה מעשרים אמה, ואז אני בעצם בונה במה באמצע הסוכה, שהסכך מרוחק ממנה פחות מעשרים אמה, וכל הדפנות יהיו על ידי דופן עקומה. אלא שיש לשים לב, בסוכה מספיק שלוש דפנות, כך שהצד הרביעי כשר עד לדופן המקורית מדין פסל היוצא מן הסוכה, למרות ששם המקום גבוה מעשרים אמה, ואני יכול לבחור מה יהיה הצד הרביעי הזה ולשבת שם. ואפילו שני אנשים שונים יכולים כל אחד להחליט מה הצד הרביעי שלו ואין כאן תרתי דסתרי!
3. ראה משנ"ב תרלג, כ-כב, ושעה"צ כג.

נשאלתי על ידי אשה שלומדת קורס של איפור קבוע שמחדירים את האיפור לשכבה הראשונה מתחת לעור ושואלת האם יש בזה איסור של כתובת קעקע?

בהחלט יש כאן בעיה וחשש לאיסור של כתובת קעקע ויש להמנע מכך.

שלום!
יש לי שקית מלא עם שיורי ד' מינים ושיורי פתילות חנוכה וכנראה הם כבר מעופשים ויש ריח..
האם מותר לזרוק אותם כיס בתוך כיס או דווקא בשריפה?
תודה

אם אתה לא יכול לשרוף, מותר לזרוק בדרך כבוד עטוף היטב. עדיף לא לשים באשפה אלא ליד האשפה.
עיין בשו"ע או"ח סימן כ"א ובמשנה ברורה סק"ו. ועיין במשנה ברורה סימן תרל"ח ס"ק כ"ד, ובסימן תרס"ד סעיף ד'.

האם יש בעייה הלכתית לאשכנזיותבביצוע עיצוב ומילוי גבות בשיטת ספריי פודרה(משום כתובת קעקע)

בהחלט יש כאן בעיה וחשש לאיסור של כתובת קעקע ויש להמנע מכך.

שלום, האם אפשר להשתמש בכירה חשמלית קרמית יחיד בחג של גולדליין לצורך הדוגמא (לא אינדוקציה) כמובן עם שעון שבת.תודה.

כירה שמופעלת על ידי שעון שבת, והיא לא אינדוקציה שאז ההפעלה נעשית על ידי הנחת הסיר, אפשר לבשל בה באופן זה בחג.
